div.p: The application of large language models (LLMs) in the field of coding is evolving rapidly: from code assistants, to autonomous coding agents, and then to generating complete projects through natural language. Early LLM code benchmarks primarily focused on code generation accuracy, but these benchmarks have gradually become saturated. Benchmark saturation weakens their guiding role for LLMs. For example, HumanEval Pass@1 has reached 99.4% and MBPP 94.2%. Among various attempts to address benchmark saturation, approaches based on software engineering have stood out, but the saturation of existing software engineering benchmarks is rapidly increasing. To address this, we propose a new benchmark, Web-Bench 12 , which contains 50 projects, each consisting of 20 tasks with sequential dependencies. The tasks implement project features in sequence, simulating real-world human development workflows. When designing Web-Bench, we aim to cover the foundational elements of Web development: Web Standards and Web Frameworks. Given the scale and complexity of these projects, which were designed by engineers with 5 to 10 years of experience, each presents a significant challenge. On average, a single project takes 4 to 8 hours for a senior engineer to complete. On our given benchmark agent (Web-Agent), SOTA (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) achieves only 25.1% Pass@1, significantly lower (better) than SWE-Bench's Verified (65.4%) and Full (33.8%) scores. Finally, we discuss that in any development field, Standards and Frameworks represent foundational knowledge and efficiency tools, respectively, and LLMs require optimization tailored to them.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The application scope of large language models (LLMs) is constantly expanding and already includes fields such as chatbots, search, and scientific research. Applications in the field of coding are also evolving rapidly, from basic code assistants [1,2], to autonomous coding agents [3], and then to attempts to generate complete projects through natural language [4,5]. Although it is still in the early stages of exploration, the potential of LLM coding is already evident despite limited practical results.

Early LLM code benchmarks focused on the accuracy of code generation, but these benchmarks have gradually become saturated: HumanEval [6] SOTA 99.4% [7] and MBPP [8] SOTA 94.2% [9]. Benchmark saturation weakens their guiding role for LLMs. To solve this problem, many new ideas have emerged, such as increasing programming languages [10,11,12], increasing test coverage [13,14], increasing dataset complexity [15,16,17,18], and improving software engineering reproducibility [19,20,21,22]. We prefer to find a method that can measure the actual complexity of codes. This means that the benchmark should cover the coding process as much as possible and be close to real projects in 1 https://github.com/bytedance/web-bench 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/bytedance-research/Web-Bench terms of logical complexity. Among many ideas, software engineering is undoubtedly the closest to this goal.

Existing software engineering benchmarks, such as SWE-Bench [22] and RepoBench [20], both use independent tasks to organize datasets. Although the data in these benchmarks may come from real projects, the tasks themselves lack coherence and differ significantly from real-world development workflows. This paper proposes a new benchmark, Web-Bench, which contains 50 projects, each consisting of 20 tasks with sequential dependencies. The tasks implement project features in sequence, simulating real-world human development workflows. When designing Web-Bench, we aim to cover the foundational elements of Web development: Web Standards and Web Frameworks. Web Standards are basic knowledge of Web development and cover CSS Selector, CSS Layout, DOM, SVG, WebGL, ECMAScript [23], TypeScript [24], etc. Web Frameworks provide higher-level abstraction capability and improve development efficiency, covering key aspects of Web development such as UI Framework [25], State Management [26], CSS Framework, Fullstack Framework, ORM, Build, etc.

Given the scale and complexity of these projects, which were designed by engineers with 5-10 years of experience, each presents a significant challenge. On average, a single project takes 4-8 hours for a senior engineer to complete. On our given benchmark agent (Web-Agent), SOTA (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) achieves only 25.1% Pass@1, significantly lower than SWE-Bench's 65.4% (Verified) [27] and 33.8% (Full). A year ago (2024.4), SWE-Bench (Verified) SOTA was only 25.6% which has increased rapidly. Table 3 below compares the SOTA of more benchmarks.

div.head: Benchmark Construction
div.p: The Web-Bench dataset contains 50 projects, each consisting of 20 tasks with sequential dependencies. See Figure 1.
1. Dataset: a collection of projects. Due to the evaluation cost, we plan to provide a Lite version in the future.
2. Project: a single item in the dataset.
3. Task: including a description and several end-toend (E2E) testcases. On average, there are 3.6 cases per task and 72.4 cases per project, as shown in Table 1.
Figure 1: Task-2 depends on the execution result ('main' element) of Task-1

During the design process of the project, different business scenarios 2 were selected: Games, Utilities, Charts, Drawing Boards, Surveys, Data Tables, Blog Sites, Document Sites, etc., so that the final Benchmark is closer to real-world software engineering. Web-Bench covers the core Web standards and mainstream development frameworks 3 4 that Web application development relies on. see Appendix A for more details. 2.2 Standard and Framework 2.2.1 Standard Web Standards are the basic knowledge of Web development, especially those that are frequently used, offer extensive functionality, and enable more complex features. We have selected the core standards that Web applications rely on, covering HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Partial core standards: • ECMAScript: the JavaScript language standard that ensures the interoperability of web pages across different web browsers. • TypeScript: A strongly typed programming language that builds on JavaScript. TypeScript code converts to JavaScript, which runs anywhere JavaScript runs. Most modern web applications are now built with TypeScript.
• CSS Selector: Patterns that match against elements in a tree and are one of the core technologies used to select nodes in a document.

• Flexbox: A layout model that arranges items in one dimension. The children of a flex container can be laid out in any direction, and can "flex" their sizes, either growing to fill unused space or shrinking to avoid overflowing the parent. It is widely used in most web applications.

• Grid: A two-dimensional grid-based layout system. The children of a grid container can be positioned into arbitrary slots in a predefined flexible or fixedsize layout grid. It is more powerful than flexbox and also widely used in web applications.
• DOM (Document Object Model): defines a platform neutral model for events and node trees. It is the main technology used to manipulate web page elements.
• SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics): An XML-based language for describing two-dimensional graphics. SVG drawings can be interactive and dynamic.
Animations can be defined and triggered declaratively.
• Canvas: Used for drawing graphics via JavaScript and the HTML <canvas> element. It can be used for animation, game graphics, data visualization, photo manipulation, and real-time video processing.
• WebGL (Web Graphic Language): An immediate mode 3D rendering API designed for the web. It is derived from OpenGL® ES 3.0, and provides similar rendering functionality, but in an HTML context.

div.head: Framework
div.p: In the early stages of Web development, there were not many development frameworks, and various Web applications could be developed using native technologies. However, with the rise of Web 2.0, both the technical complexity and application scale of Web applications have increased dramatically, and the development efficiency based solely on native Web technology has been challenged. Development frameworks have brought greater abstraction capabilities, improved development efficiency, and enhanced collaboration to Web development, covering its main aspects:

• UI Framework: Usually provides a componentbased development model and supporting development tools to improve the efficiency of singleunit development and collaboration, such as React, Vue, Angular, Threejs, etc.

• State Management: UI state management is one of the core tasks in Web application development. Excellent frameworks will simplify the state model and improve development and maintenance efficiency, such as Redux, Zustand, Jotai, Mobx, etc.

• CSS Framework: Improves CSS maintainability and development efficiency by enhancing basic capabilities such as variables, modules, functions, or providing CSS utilities. Examples include SASS, LESS, Stylus, Tailwind, etc.

• Build: Web applications eventually run in browsers, and during the development phase, JS code and various resources (CSS, images, icons etc.) are usually split into many modules (or files), which require modular packaging using build tools, as well as optimization such as merging and compression. At the same time, build tools are also required to unify the development experiencehandling JS syntax conversion, CSS preprocessing, and integration of various tools (including linting, formatting, testing frameworks, etc.) -such as Webpack, Vite, Parcel, etc.

• Fullstack Framework: Fullstack usually refers to the ability of developers to handle both front-end (such as UI) and back-end (such as data and logic processing) development. In this context, it refers to frameworks that support both front-end and back-end development, such as Next.js, Nuxt, Express.js, etc.

• Database Framework Data management is a relatively independent and core part of back-end logic. Data can be managed directly via SQL using tools like SQLite, or through object-relational mapping frameworks such as Prisma and Sequelize.

div.head: Calibrate Project
div.p: Use Web-Bench evaluation tool to Calibrate a project. More details can be found in Appendix D. That is, check for design issues in the project:
1. Task issues, such as ambiguous descriptions, vulnerabilities, or obvious conflicts with testcases.
2. Testcase issues, such as not rigorous enough or too strict.

Test: end-to-end (E2E) test with Playwright. 8. Retry: with error context from Build or Test.

div.head: Evaluator Workflow
div.p: (a) First attempt, if failed, implement task-n with task description and error context, goto step-3.
(b) Second attempt, if failed, evaluation is done.

div.head: Web-Agent Workflow
div.p: Web-Agent is an instance of the agent described in Section 3.2, Step 3. Web-Agent is the interaction module between Web-Bench and LLM. Its main responsibilities are to build prompts, request LLM API, and extract files from LLM response. 1. Build Prompts: Using system prompt (SP), task description, files, and error messages. If the combined input exceeds the context length, it will be truncated. 2. Request LLM: As shown in Table 2. Requests the LLM's OpenAPI based on the selected model and returns the response. In this step, parameters such as temperature, maxToken, contextLength are obtained from the model provider. 3. Extract Files: Parses the LLM's response to extract the generated files.
More details can be found in Appendix B.
Metrics
• Percentage of tasks passing all E2E tests on the first attempt.
• pass_tasks@1: number of tasks passed on first attempt before any failure.
• tasks: total number of tasks in 'tasks.jsonl'. • pass_tasks@2: total number of passed tasks including retries.
Example:
• tasks: 20
• pass_tasks@1: 5, the first failed evaluation happened at task-6
• pass_tasks@2: 15, total passed tasks is 15 (task-16's second attempt failed)

div.head: Evaluation Results
div.p: As shown in Figure 7, 'claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219thinking' achieves the highest Pass@1 and Pass@2 (using Best-of-5 sampling, as used throughout). From the Pass@1 distribution, Claude-series models exhibit the highest performance, followed by GPT, Doubao, DeepSeek, LLAMA, Gemini, Qwen, and others. From the Pass@2 distribution, Claude-series models exhibit the highest performance, followed by Doubao, DeepSeek, GPT, Gemini, LLAMA, Mistral, and others.

As shown in Figure 7 and 8, regardless of Pass@1 or Pass@2, closed-source models (shown in red) also appear to have an advantage. As shown in Figure 9, the average Pass@2 of closed models is 20.79%, while that of open models is 14.84%. The average Pass@1 of closed models is 15.08%, while that of open models is 10.73%.
More details can be found in Appendix E.

As shown in Figure 10 and 11, the Pass@2 distribution across LLM series indicates that newer or largerparameter models generally perform better in Web-Bench, which aligns with the commonly observed scaling law. Figure 10: Pass@2 across LLMs within the same model series -Part 1 Figure 11: Pass@2 across LLMs within the same model series -Part 2

As shown in Figure 12, LLMs of the same specification perform better on Pass@2 when the thinking mode is enabled. 4.2 Compare SOTAs As shown in Table 3 and Figure 13, HumanEval and MBPP have approached saturation. APPS and EvalPlus are approaching saturation. The SOTA for Web-Bench is 25.1%, which is lower (better) than that of the SWE-bench Full and Verified sets.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Early LLM code benchmarks focused on the accuracy of single-function code generation. We review several widely cited benchmarks:

• HumanEval [6]: 164 handwritten Python coding questions are used to evaluate functional correctness. Each question contains a function signature, docstring, and function body, and has an average of 7.7 test cases.
• MBPP [8]: About 1,000 entry-level crowd-sourced Python coding questions covering coding basics and standard library functions, with each question having an average of 3 test cases.

• APPS [29]: 10,000 Python coding questions-5,000 for training and 5,000 for testing-sourced from multiple coding competition websites, covering simple problems, technical interview questions, and algorithm competition-level challenges. Each question has an average of 13 test cases. From Table 3, we can see that HumanEval is saturated, and MBPP is close to saturation. APPS performs slightly better due to its larger dataset size, but it is also approaching saturation. To address code benchmark saturation, many new ideas have emerged.

div.head: Increase programming languages
div.p: Most of the problems in early code benchmarks used Python as the programming language. In addition to Python, mainstream languages in real-world development include C++, JavaScript, Java, Go, etc., making it natural to consider expanding language coverage.
• MultiPL-E [10] translates HumanEval and MBPP to 18 other programming languages.
• HumanEval-X [11] extends the HumanEval benchmark to Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, and Go via human translations

• HumanEvalPack [12] extends the HumanEval benchmark to cover three coding tasks-code repair, code interpretation, and code generation-and six languages (Python, JavaScript, Java, Go, C++, Rust) via human translations. As shown in Table 3, the SOTA in 2024 has reached 78%.

div.head: Increase test coverage
div.p: This stems from a simple idea: improving test coverage and increasing the presence of edge cases is expected to reduce the pass rate.

• CodeContests [13] is a competitive coding dataset for machine learning. It automatically generates additional test cases (mutations), such as bit flipping of input strings or integer addition and subtraction. It uses multiple correct solutions to verify the new tests and ensure consistent output, and filters out problems with insufficient or overly simple test cases.

• EvalPlus [14] detects the robustness of generated code by strengthening the scope and number of HumanEval and MBPP tests. For the same LLM, Pass@1 can generally be reduced by 5-10%. However, as shown in Table 3, the latest SOTA has reached 89%, gradually approaching saturation.

div.head: Increasing dataset complexity
div.p: The problems in the early code benchmarks contain many basic algorithms, which are no longer challenging for LLMs; increasing the complexity of a single problem is also an idea.

• DS-1000 [15] is a code generation benchmark containing 1,000 data science problems, covering seven Python libraries such as NumPy and Pandas. The problems come from Stackoverflow and have been lightly edited.

• CoderEval [16] contains 230 Python and 230 Java code generation problems carefully selected from popular open source projects. It supports code generation problems with six different levels of context dependency. It supports problems with six levels of context dependency, and performance is significantly better when generating independent functions compared to non-independent ones.

• BigCodeBench [17] combines tools from 139 libraries across 7 domains to support 1,140 finegrained tasks. It integrates multiple existing benchmarks and enables the implementation of functions such as data analysis and web development by calling multiple tools.

• MLE-bench [18] is a benchmark for measuring the performance of AI agents in machine learning engineering tasks. 75 ML engineering competitions were selected from Kaggle to evaluate real-world skills such as model training, dataset preparation, and running experiments for machine learning workflows. As shown in Table 3, the current SOTA is only 16.9%. As the coding capabilities of LLMs continue to improve, such professionally oriented benchmarks are expected to become more prevalent.

div.head: Improving software engineering reproducibility
div.p: Some benchmarks simulate the software engineering process from different perspectives:

• CodeXGLUE [19] includes 14 datasets for 10 diverse programming language tasks including codecode, text-code, code-text and text-text scenarios. Provides three baseline models to support these tasks, including a BERT-style pre-trained model for understanding tasks, a GPT-style pretrained model for code completion and generation, and an encoder-decoder framework that supports sequence-to-sequence generation.

• RepoBench [20] is a new benchmark containing three subtasks (RepoBench-R retrieval, RepoBench-C completion, RepoBench-P pipeline), supporting Python and Java, and covering the evaluation of automatic code completion systems at the code repository level.

• DevBench [21] is based on the waterfall model. It explores the performance of the evaluated model across five stages: software design, environment configuration, implementation, acceptance testing, and unit testing.
• SWE-bench [22] focuses on solving real and complex software engineering problems. 2,294 tasks come from 12 popular Python libraries on GitHub.

The filtering rules are as follows: approximately 90,000 Pull Requests were collected, each associated with a code base. A GitHub issue was resolved, the test files in the repository were modified, at least one test case was included, and the test status changed from failed to passed. SWEbench offers substantial scale and real-world software engineering complexity. In the past two years, it has gradually become a highly cited code benchmark. As shown in Table 3, after two years, the SOTA-especially on the Full set-remains far from saturation.

div.head: Why Software Engineering?
div.p: Based on the discussion in Chapter 5 and the SOTA data presented in Table 3:

Increasing the types of programming languages cannot solve the benchmark saturation problem. This is intuitive. Real-world programming languages have their own characteristics and strengths, but are similar in expressiveness. In fact, LLM pass rates across different language versions of the same benchmark do not vary significantly [12].

Increasing test coverage seems to have some effect, but EvalPlus [14] also approached saturation within two years of its publication. Although CodeContests [13] performs better, its unsaturated SOTA is likely due to the high difficulty of its competition-level question set. Similarly, in real-world scenarios, project complexity arises from factors such as lines of code, code logic complexity, and the structure of the module/component dependency tree. Even 100% test coverage cannot change the complexity of the project itself.

Increasing the complexity of the dataset-whether by increasing the complexity of individual problems [16,18] or by expanding the scale of the benchmark [17]-appears effective based on SOTA results. However, the upper limit of this approach often consists of uncommon and complex algorithmic problems, which gradually deviate from real-world coding. This may lead LLM coding to evolve in a less practical direction.

Simulating the software engineering process has been theoretically demonstrated as feasible by CodeXGLUE, RepoBench, and DevBench. These benchmarks have also been preliminarily validated on earlier LLMs, paving the way for larger-scale software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench and Web-Bench. Benchmarks in the software engineering direction are grounded in real-world coding behaviors.
Web-Bench is a new software engineering benchmark and fills the gap: Sequential task evaluation for fullstack web development based on Web standards and frameworks. 4

div.head: LLMs require optimization tailored to Standards and Frameworks
div.p: Referring to the previous section, we note that software engineering provides a promising solution to benchmark saturation. Furthermore, if the problems contained in the benchmark (or in the projects presented in this work) accurately reflect real-world code, they can help guide LLMs to evolve in a practical direction. A fundamental question arises: what is the basis of real-world coding? Although this article primarily discusses web application development, the development process in any field [30] is fundamentally built upon standards (also referred to as protocols, specifications, or recommendations) and frameworks (which may include libraries or third-party packages). Standards and Frameworks represent the basic knowledge and efficiency tools in a coding field, respectively. From this perspective, they are universally applicable. So we have an intuition: LLM needs optimization tailored to Standards and Frameworks.
We are also conducting further in-depth research in this direction, which may serve as a potential breakthrough in the next stage:
1. Standards-aware Training:
• Inject W3C/WHATWG documentation into pretraining data.
• Finetune with AST based syntax constraint checks.

div.head: Framework-specific Adaptation:
div.p: • Add framework rule checkers to decoding loops.

• Develop plugin architectures for framework updates (avoiding retraining). This paper mainly studies the accuracy of code generation for LLMs. We have also received feedback from users on multiple occasions expressing interest in evaluating the aesthetics and code quality of the generated pages. Since the evaluation of aesthetics and code quality can largely reuse the existing benchmark infrastructure, Web-Bench already includes a built-in screenshot function. In the future, it can be easily extended to support additional metrics.

div.head: A.1.1 UI Framework
div.p: UI frameworks offer component-based development, which can improve the efficiency of developing complicated web frontend application.
We have four projects: React, Vue, Angular, and Svelte, which represent four popular UI frameworks. These projects share the same tasks, and here is the pass@2 (Best of Five) for these projects:

div.head: React Vue Angular Svelte
div.p: Claude-3.

7-Tfoot_1 60 40 50 55 Claude-3.7foot_2 65 30 40 25 Doubao-1.5-Tfoot_3 50 40 25 40 Doubao-1.5foot_4 35 35 5 10 GPT-4o 35 30 5 20 DeepSeek-R1 40 30 30 40 Analysis The following presents an analysis of these evaluation results: 1. When compared to Vue (208k stars), Angular (96k stars), and Svelte (79k stars), React (235k stars) is the most widely-used UI framework in the web domain and provides the largest dataset for LLM training. 2. React supports the JSX language feature, which combines JavaScript and HTML, thereby enhancing data density. 3. Vue/Svelte exhibits similarities to HTML grammar and demonstrates superior performance in certain models. 4. Angular features the most complex grammar, making it difficult for LLMs to learn and utilize.

div.head: A.1.2 State Management
div.p: State management framework provides a structured and efficient approach for managing state changes.

We have four projects: Redux, Mobx, Zustand, and Jotai, which represent four popular state management frameworks. These projects share the same tasks, and here is the pass@2 (Best of Five) for these projects:

Analysis The following presents an analysis of these evaluation results: 1. Zustand demonstrates superior performance compared to other state-management frameworks, which can be attributed to its popularity and simple API design.
2. Mobx is easy to use, but also easy to make mistakes. For example, Mobx users may forget to add the observer higher-order component (HOC).

div.head: Zustand, Jotai, Mobx features a clean and straightforward API design.
A.1.3 Fullstack Framework
div.p: Fullstack Framework empowers developers to construct both the front-end and back-end components of a web application.

There are five projects available to demonstrate the large language model's (LLM) ability to implement fullstack applications. These projects encompass Nextjs, Nuxt, Expressjs, Fastify, and FastifyReact. These projects share the same tasks, and here is the pass@2 (Best of Five) for these projects:

Express Fastify F * 12foot_5 Claude-3.7-T 35 25 40 40 35 Claude-3.7 40 25 45 40 35 Doubao-1.5-T 20 20 35 45 35 Doubao-1.5 15 20 50 15 5 GPT-4o 10 25 40 20 5 DeepSeek-R1 20 25 25 20 25 Analysis The following presents an analysis of these evaluation results: 1. Expressjs has the longest history (since 2010) in the fullstack domain, and its API is clean and stable across versions. 2. Although Nextjs has the highest number of stars, its API is not stable across different versions, and large language models (LLMs) may be confused by the differences between Server Components and Client Components. 3. When comparing Next and Nuxt: React-based Next is better than Vue-based Nuxt. 4. Fastify-React exhibits poor performance in simple tasks: React Router v7 in Fastify-React is a breaking change version update compared with v6, and in this case, react-router-dom is not required, yet LLMs often overlook this fact.

div.head: A.1.4 Database
div.p: The database is crucial for the backend logic in a fullstack application. Developers can access the database through various Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) tools or Database APIs.

We present four projects (Sequelize, NoSQL, Prisma, and Lowdb) to showcase the Large Language Model's (LLM) capability to utilize ORM/Database APIs. These projects share the same tasks, and here is the pass@2 (Best of Five) for these projects:

Model Sequelize NoSQL Prisma Lowdb Claude-3.7-T 40 35 10 35 Claude-3.7 40 40 45 50 Doubao-1.5-T 20 35 25 30 Doubao-1.5 25 20 25 30 GPT-4o 20 25 5 25 DeepSeek-R1 40 35 20 30 Analysis The following presents an analysis of these evaluation results: 1. Nosql exhibits good performance. The Document Model of MongoDB is significantly easier to use than that of relation-based databases, and it is also suitable for Node.js. 2. Lowdb is an extremely simple JSON database. With lowdb, database APIs are the same as JavaScript Array APIs, which is simple enough for LLM to understand.

div.head: A.2 Flex
div.p: Definition from W3C:

The specification describes a CSS box model optimized for user interface design. In the flex layout model, the children of a flex container can be laid out in any direction, and can "flex" their sizes, either growing to fill unused space or shrinking to avoid overflowing the parent. Both horizontal and vertical alignment of the children can be easily manipulated. Nesting of these boxes (horizontal inside vertical, or vertical inside horizontal) can be used to build layouts in two dimensions.

div.head: from MDN:
div.p: The CSS flexible box layout module defines a CSS box model optimized for user interface design, and the layout of items in one dimension. In the flex layout model, the children of a flex container can be laid out in any direction, and can "flex" their sizes, either growing to fill unused space or shrinking to avoid overflowing the parent. Both horizontal and vertical alignment of the children can be easily manipulated.

div.p: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces.

-Declarative: React makes it painless to create interactive UIs. Design simple views for each state in your application, and React will efficiently update and render just the right components when your data changes. Declarative views make your code more predictable, simpler to understand, and easier to debug.

-Component-Based: Build encapsulated components that manage their own state, then compose them to make complex UIs. Since component logic is written in JavaScript instead of templates, you can easily pass rich data through your app and keep the state out of the DOM.

-Learn Once, Write Anywhere: We don't make assumptions about the rest of your technology stack, so you can develop new features in React without rewriting existing code. React can also render on the server using Node and power mobile apps using React Native.

div.head: System Prompt
div.p: When generating new code : 1. Always produce a single code block . 2. Never separate the code into multiple code blocks . 3. Only include the code that is being added . 4. No explanation , no issue , only code . 5. Never omit any code . , 6. If the user submits a code block that contains a filename in the language specifier , always include the filename in any code block you generate based on that file . The filename should be on the next line as the language specifier in your code block . 7. Don 't repeat filename in code block . Always follow these guidelines when generating code responses . Task Description add divs ( class ' header ' , ' footer ' , ' content ') with arbitrary text in '. root ' element . '. root ' occupies total viewport and children elements together occupy total '. root ' space . header ( border -box ) is always fixed at the top of '. root '; footer ( borderbox ) is always fixed at the bottom of '. root '; content ( border -box ) occupies the remaining '. root ' space . USE tailwind grid only , NO flex , float and position , NO js . Add new model for evaluation 1. For models deployed on OpenRouter, use the native OpenRouter provider with the following configuration: { " title " : " anthropic / claude -3 -opus " , " provider " : " openrouter " , " model " : " anthropic / claude -3 -opus " , " apiBase " : " https :// openrouter . ai / api / v1 " , " apiKey " : " {{ OPENROUTER_API_KEY }} " } 2. If existing providers do not meet your requirements, you can evaluate specific models by creating a new Provider. This is achieved by extending the BaseLLM:

abstract class BaseLLM { abstract provider : string abstract option : LLMOption info : Model abstract chat ( compiledMessages : ChatMessage [] , originOptions : CompletionOptions ) : Promise <{ request : string error ?: string response : string } > } 1. option -define parameters for LLM requests: export interface LLMOption { contextLength : number maxTokens : number temperature ?: number apiBase : string } 2. info -model metadata in apps/eval/src/model.json. 3. chat -custom request method that returns the generated text from the LLM. Use custom agent for evaluation Web-Bench supports custom agent by built-in HTTP-Agent. During the "Call Agent" step 3.2, the HTTP-Agent will: 1. Pass the Evaluator's context to your CustomAgent. 2. Return the CustomAgent's response to the Evaluator without modifications. The request and response formats can be found in the next section. C.2 C.2 Agent Data Format HTTP Request HTTP Request Method POST HTTP Request Body export interface AgentRequest { type : " normal " | " init " task : string // Code files , key is filePath , value is fileContent files ?: Record < string , string > // Error context error ?: string }
